dedupe_keys.name: manrs mutually agreed norms for routing security and its measured effect

description: This policy and operations case covers MANRS, a voluntary programme in which network operators, internet exchange points, content and cloud providers and equipment vendors commit to basic routing security actions: filtering incorrect routes, preventing spoofed traffic, keeping contact details up to date and publishing routing policy in registries and RPKI. Launched in 2014 and supported by the Internet Society, it passed 1,000 participants in 2023 (1,073 at the end of that year) and runs an observatory that scores conformance from public routing data. Its community reports and research based on it find that MANRS members are more likely to register their routes: about 66 per cent of participants had valid Route Origin Authorizations against 34 per cent of networks globally, and 60.1 per cent of member networks originated only RPKI-valid routes against 24.7 per cent of others. An exchange programme asks route servers to filter, and the programme description cites studies suggesting that when exchanges began dropping RPKI-invalid routes in 2018 many networks fixed their records. MANRS logged more than 1,430 routing incidents in 2020. Coverage: global, 2014 onward. Format and access: website, observatory and annual community reports as PDF, free. Caveats: participation is voluntary and self-selected, so comparisons do not prove cause; figures differ between reports and years. Simulation uses: policy scenarios for routing security, the share of networks filtering in hijack propagation models, and operational norms at exchanges. Related records: the Rostelecom and Pakistan hijacks, RIPE RIS, BGPStream and BGPy.
